claims.text: A two-phase direct-coexistence approach within ab initio molecular dynamics can calculate melting properties of high-melting materials.
The direct-coexistence approach can accurately calculate melting temperature.
The direct-coexistence approach can calculate the enthalpy and entropy of fusion.
The direct-coexistence approach can calculate the volume change at the melting point.
The direct-coexistence approach has significantly lower computational cost than full ab initio free-energy integration.
A suitable implementation uses a simulation cell containing coexisting solid and liquid phases and performs ab initio molecular dynamics near the expected melting temperature.
Sufficiently large supercells are required to maintain and sample solid-liquid coexistence.
Constant-pressure NPT simulations can be used while monitoring energy, volume, and structure to identify the equilibrium melting point and associated thermodynamic properties.
Placing solid and liquid in the same simulation cell forms a solid-liquid interface that permits in situ observation of melting-related changes.
When the solid and liquid phases equilibrate, a stable interface reveals the melting temperature.
The enthalpy of fusion can be extracted from the enthalpy difference between the coexisting solid and liquid phases.
The entropy of fusion can be obtained from thermodynamic differences between the coexisting phases at melting.
The volume change at melting can be extracted from the volume difference between the coexisting phases.
Direct-coexistence results can achieve accuracy close to full ab initio free-energy calculations.
The reduced computational cost makes the method more feasible for high-throughput exploration of refractory materials.
Full ab initio thermodynamic integration provides high accuracy but requires computationally prohibitive sampling across the temperature range.
Accuracy may degrade for materials with strong anharmonicity, significant nuclear quantum effects, or very large supercell requirements.
For many metals, predicted melting temperatures from the method typically deviate by only a few percent.
The error depends on the material and simulation parameters.
